title: Start Here
blurb: Read this first: what you need, the units, and your first session step by step.
html:
In short

  • This block lasts 12 weeks.
  • You will train three times a week and walk more.
  • Start light and learn each exercise before adding weight.
  • Use the Oraimo watch and the tracker on your phone to record what you do.

What this playbook is for

This block runs from Monday 16 November 2026 to Sunday 7 February 2027, after a lead-in weekend on Saturday 14 and Sunday 15 November. Its main goal is to build the habit of training three times a week and walking more. Fat loss and muscle gain come second.

What you need

You need a flat bench, a pair of 8.5 kg dumbbells, a barbell with plates, a mat or towel, a water bottle, a bathroom scale, a tape measure, your Oraimo watch and the tracker on your phone. A kilogram (kg) is a unit of weight.

Claude is the AI assistant you chat with. You can tell it your numbers and it logs them for you. The tracker has four tabs at the bottom: Week shows today's workout, Guide holds this playbook, Progress shows your charts, and Log is where you save the day. Your Oraimo watch shows steps and sleep in its phone app. A Telegram message each Sunday evening scores your week.

Units used in this playbook

  • kg means kilogram, about the weight of a 1-litre bottle of water.
  • g means gram. A gram is a thousandth of a kg. A small egg weighs about 50 g in total and holds about 6 g of protein, the nutrient that builds and repairs tissue.
  • lb means pound, about 0.45 kg.
  • cm means centimetre and in means inch. An inch is about 2.5 cm.
  • L means litre, a unit used for drinks.
  • kcal means kilocalorie, the "calories" shown on food labels. A calorie measures energy in food and drink.
  • Steps are counted by your Oraimo watch.

Five words you will see everywhere

Rep: A rep, short for repetition, is one complete exercise movement.

Set: A set is a group of reps done before a rest. Three sets of ten reps means you do ten reps, rest, and repeat that twice.

Reps in Reserve: Reps in Reserve (RIR) means the number of good reps you could still do when you stop a set. A good rep uses the full movement at a steady speed, without swinging, changing your back position or feeling pain.

Warm-up: A warm-up is five minutes of easy movement before training. It prepares your muscles and joints.

Cool-down: A cool-down is five minutes of gentle stretches after training.

Your first session, step by step

Saturday 14 November is Strength A. Open the tracker. The Week tab shows the session.

  1. Warm up for 5 minutes with the videos in Current Program.
  2. For each exercise, watch the video once and read its steps in How to Do Each Exercise.
  3. Do 3 sets of 8–12 reps with the starting weight. Stop each set when you could still do 1–3 more good reps. You train alone with no rack, so never go until you cannot finish a rep.
  4. Rest 60–120 seconds between sets.
  5. Cool down with the stretches in the programme.
  6. Log the weight and the number of reps in the tracker's Log tab, or tell Claude.

Expect the exercises to feel awkward at first. The first two weeks are for learning them.

Staying safe

Stop a set if you feel sharp pain or pain in a joint. Muscle effort and mild burning are normal. Mild muscle soreness 1–2 days later is also normal.

You train alone with no rack. Stop each set when you could still do 1–3 more good reps. Never go until you cannot finish a rep. If you get stuck during the Bench Press, lower the bar to your chest, roll it down your body to your hips and sit up.

See a doctor before starting if you have chest pain, dizziness, high blood pressure or a past injury.

Where to go next

  • Current Program tells you what to do each day.
  • How to Do Each Exercise gives step-by-step exercise instructions.
  • Daily Checklist gives you the boxes to tick each day.
  • Glossary explains unfamiliar words.

title: Goals and Foundations
blurb: Why train, how to set a goal, and the beginner myths to ignore.
html:
In short

  • Fitness supports your energy, strength, health, mood, focus and sleep.
  • Choose one clear goal and a realistic time period.
  • This block uses three strength sessions each week and about 1,850 kcal a day to lose about 0.5 kg a week.
  • Consistent training, food, sleep and recovery matter more than body type.

What to do

In this block you eat about 1,850 kilocalories (kcal) a day to lose about 0.5 kg a week. Walk to your step target, eat about 120 g of protein, lift three times a week and sleep 7 hours. Then watch your weekly weight average.

  1. Use this goal: "Complete three strength sessions a week for 12 weeks, from Monday 16 November 2026 to Sunday 7 February 2027."
  2. Follow the sessions in Current Program. Resistance means weight your muscles push or pull against. This block uses your body weight, dumbbells and barbell as resistance.
  3. Check steps on the Oraimo watch, eat to the calorie and protein targets, and sleep for 7 or more hours.
  4. Start with Start Here, then complete the first Strength A session.

Why fitness matters

Fitness supports a high-performing life and can also change how you look. A consistent routine helps your heart, bones, muscles and joints. It can improve mood, focus, confidence, sleep, discipline and your sense of control.

Bone density means how much mineral your bones contain. Denser bones are usually stronger.

BenefitImpact
EnergyBetter focus, motivation and stamina through the day.
StrengthMove better, lift things, lower injury risk.
ProtectionStronger immune system and lower risk of heart disease, diabetes and depression.

The body works like a business. Food, rest and movement are the inputs. Metabolism is how the body turns food into energy and keeps itself working. Hormones and mental state also affect the system. The results include strength, focus, confidence and well-being.

Starting late

Age, weight and current fitness do not block progress. The body can adapt at any stage. Early wins build confidence. Small actions, such as walking more and drinking more water, add up. A habit is easier to keep than a health crisis is to fix.

Setting goals

Vague goals such as "get fit" or "lose weight" often fade. Use a Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound (SMART) goal.

  • "Lose 5 kg of fat in 10 weeks through strength training and calorie control."
  • "Build visible upper-body muscle over 3 months with 3 workouts a week."

The worked SMART goal for this block is specific because it names strength training, measurable because you count three sessions each week, achievable with the home equipment, relevant to building the habit, and time-bound by the 12-week dates.

Pick a time horizon

TimeframeFocusExample
Short term (4–12 weeks)Habits and disciplineWork out 3 times a week for 6 weeks.
Long term (6–12 months)Bigger changeLose 10 kg and run a 10K, a 10-kilometre run, in 6 months.

Health goals and looks goals

Both are valid. Health goals cover heart health, mobility, stamina and blood pressure. Looks goals cover how clothes fit, posture and definition. One usually leads to the other. Strength training, for example, brings definition and fat loss.

Start where you are

Do not copy an athlete's routine or a friend's meal plan. Assess your current level, choose a realistic starting point and let goals change as you grow.

Myths and beginner mistakes

Myth or mistakeBetter belief
You can spot-reduce fatFat loss is whole-body. Sit-ups do not flatten the stomach unless overall body fat drops.
Cardio is better than weights for fat lossCardio burns calories during the session. Lifting keeps muscle while you diet. Do both.
Weights make you bulkyLarge muscle takes years of hard training and eating. Most people get leaner and more defined. Women gain bone density and a better body composition from lifting too.
You must train every dayMuscle grows and fat is lost during recovery. This block uses 3 structured sessions a week.
Copying random routinesFollow a structured beginner plan that teaches movement patterns, builds core strength and builds consistency.
The scale tells everythingWeight moves with water, digestion, hormones and muscle. Track several measures (see Tracking and Habits).
Ignoring diet, sleep and stressYou cannot out-train a bad diet, poor sleep or chronic stress.

On cardio versus weights: lifting does not raise your metabolism much. A kilo of muscle burns only about 13 kilocalories a day at rest (see Fat Loss and Metabolism). The case for lifting in a diet is keeping muscle and shape. The case for cardio and walking is the calories they burn and heart health.

On overtraining: beginners rarely overtrain from lifting. When people feel run down, the cause is usually poor sleep, too little food and life stress. See Recovery, Stress and Mobility.

Deeper reading (optional)

You do not need this for the first 12 weeks.

Different food targets: Fat loss uses a calorie deficit, meaning you eat less energy than you burn. Muscle gain uses a calorie surplus, meaning you eat more. Body recomposition means losing fat and gaining muscle together near maintenance, where you eat about the energy you burn. Lean mass means everything in the body that is not fat. Cutting and bulking are informal names for fat-loss and muscle-gain phases.

Sheldon's three body types, called ectomorph, mesomorph and endomorph, are not supported by evidence. Genetics can change how fast you respond to training and diet, but the basic rules stay the same. Everyone needs a calorie balance that fits the goal, enough protein, progressively harder training and good sleep.

title: Fat Loss and Metabolism
blurb: How fat loss works, where your daily calories go, and why steps matter.
html:
In short

  • You lose fat by burning more calories than you eat.
  • Daily movement can change your calorie burn more than another workout.
  • Strength training helps you keep muscle while losing fat.
  • Sleep supports hunger control, energy and training quality.
  • Use weekly trends because water and normal body changes can hide fat loss.

What to do

In this block you eat about 1,850 kilocalories (kcal) a day to lose about 0.5 kg a week. Walk to your step target, eat about 120 g of protein, lift three times a week and sleep 7 hours. Then watch your weekly weight average.

  1. Walk to the daily step target in Current Program. Check it on the Oraimo watch or the phone's Health app.
  2. Eat about 1,850 kcal a day, with 120 grams (g) of protein. Protein is the nutrient that builds and repairs tissue. Send Claude a photo of every meal so the tracker can add it up.
  3. Lift weights three times a week.
  4. Sleep for at least 7 hours.
  5. Weigh yourself on 2 or 3 mornings. Add the weights and divide by the number of mornings to get the weekly average. If it falls by about 0.5 kg a week, carry on. If it stays flat for 3 weeks of logged meals, lower the target by about 150 kcal or add 1,000 steps a day. If it falls faster than 1 kg a week, eat about 150 kcal more. One heavy morning means nothing because water and food change your weight.

A calorie is a unit of energy in food and drink. Photo estimates of meals can be 20–30% off, so the weekly weight trend, not any single day's number, tells you whether the target is right.

Deeper reading (optional)

You do not need this for the first 12 weeks.

How fat loss works

Fat (adipose tissue) stores spare energy. You gain it when you eat more calories than you burn and lose it when you burn more than you eat. Think of a bank. Food is the deposit. Activity and metabolism are the withdrawals.

A calorie deficit is the one proven way to lose fat. You can create it by eating less, moving more or both.

A pound of fat (0.45 kg) holds roughly 3,500 kilocalories. A daily deficit of 500 kilocalories is therefore about a pound a week as a starting estimate. The real long-term loss is smaller, because the body adapts as you lose weight and burns less. Use the number to set a first target, then adjust from your weekly weight average.

Your first target was set this way. At 30 years old, 80 kg and 1.71 m, your body burns about 1,720 kcal a day at complete rest (the Mifflin-St Jeor estimate). Light activity, meaning three short sessions a week and a few thousand steps a day, multiplies that by about 1.375, so you burn about 2,370 kcal a day. Eating about 1,850 kcal leaves a gap of about 520 kcal a day, which is about 0.5 kg a week. If your weekly weight average isn't falling by about that much after 2 or 3 weeks of logged meals, the estimate is off and the target moves.

Daily energy burn

Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE) is everything you burn in a day. It has four parts.

ComponentRough share of TDEEWhat it is
Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR)60–70%What you burn at rest for breathing, brain and organs. Set by age, weight, sex, height and lean mass.
Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis (NEAT)15–20%Movement outside workouts: walking, standing, chores, fidgeting.
Exercise Activity Thermogenesis (EAT)10–15%Calories burned in structured workouts.
Thermic Effect of Food (TEF)5–10%Energy used to digest and absorb food.

These are rough ranges. NEAT varies the most between people, and it is the part a sedentary person can change fastest. That is why daily steps matter more than another cardio session. Walking 8,000–10,000 steps a day adds meaningful burn, especially alongside strength training. A one-hour workout may burn 300–500 calories, but sitting the rest of the day limits the total.

Protein has the highest thermic effect.

MacronutrientShare of its calories burned in digestion
Protein20–30%
Carbohydrate5–10%
Fat0–3%

Afterburn

Excess Post-Exercise Oxygen Consumption (EPOC), the "afterburn", is real but small. It is a small fraction of the workout's own calories. Do not choose High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) for the afterburn.

Ways to raise daily calorie burn

Modestly, and not with gimmicks.

  • Stay active through the day to raise NEAT.
  • Eat enough protein to raise TEF.
  • Sleep well so appetite and energy stay steady.
  • Build muscle, with realistic expectations. A kilo of muscle burns about 13 kilocalories a day at rest, so 2 kg of new muscle adds about 25 kilocalories a day.

Green tea and fat burners have no meaningful effect.

Why muscle matters in a deficit

Lift in a deficit to keep muscle and shape, not to raise metabolism. Strength training:

  • Preserves muscle while you lose fat.
  • Prevents a "skinny-fat" look.
  • Improves insulin sensitivity.
  • Makes the weight you lose mostly fat.

Why fat loss slows

Fast early results followed by a plateau is normal.

  • Metabolic adaptation: the body becomes more efficient and burns less.
  • Water weight drops in the first 1–2 weeks.
  • NEAT falls because you move less when you eat less.

The practical response in this block is the weekly-average rule above. A diet break is a planned period at maintenance calories and is not part of this block.

Signs you are losing fat when the scale is flat

  • Looser clothes
  • Better muscle definition
  • More energy
  • Better workout performance
  • Better sleep and mood

Hormones

Get sleep, calories and training right and the hormones follow. Chasing individual hormones adds little.

Testosterone and growth hormone: Short rises after a workout do not predict muscle growth. Do not train or fast to chase them. Lifting, sleep, enough food and a healthy body weight are the useful levers. Supplements sold as testosterone boosters work only for people who are medically deficient.

Insulin: Calories decide fat gain or loss, not insulin from carbohydrates. Controlled feeding studies that match calories show similar fat loss on high-carb and low-carb diets. Strength training, protein, fibre and sleep improve insulin sensitivity.

Cortisol and stress: Everyday stress affects body fat mostly through sleep, appetite and food choices. There is no separate cortisol path to belly fat in healthy people. Clinically high cortisol is a medical problem for a doctor.

Leptin and ghrelin: These hormones affect fullness and hunger.

HormoneRoleWhat helps
LeptinTells the brain you are fullSleep, stable body weight
GhrelinSignals hungerSleep, protein, fibre

Short sleep raises ghrelin and lowers leptin. Hunger and cravings go up.

Summary

PrincipleWhy it matters
Calorie deficitThe only proven way to lose fat
Strength trainingKeeps muscle and shape in a deficit
NEAT firstDaily movement adds up faster than extra cardio
TDEEShows how the body spends energy
SleepControls hunger and training quality
Several metricsThe scale is not the full picture

See Nutrition and Supplements for calorie and protein targets and Recovery, Stress and Mobility for sleep.

The optional detail above explains the 500 kcal and 3,500 kcal estimate, the parts of daily energy use, digestion cost, afterburn, metabolic adaptation and hormones. These numbers explain the system and set this block's 1,850 kcal target.

title: Muscle and Training
blurb: How muscle grows: reps, sets, reps in reserve and adding weight.
html:
In short

  • Muscles grow when training becomes harder and recovery supports repair.
  • A rep is one movement. A set is a group of reps before a rest.
  • Stop each set when you could still do 1–3 more good reps.
  • Add reps or weight over time while keeping good form.
  • Every session works your whole body.

What to do

  1. Train your whole body three times a week with Current Program. Other plans use upper-body and lower-body splits, but this block uses full-body sessions.
  2. Do 3 sets of 8–12 reps. A rep is one complete movement. A set is a group of reps before a rest.
  3. Stop each set when you could still do 1–3 more good reps. You train alone with no rack, so never go until you cannot finish a rep.
  4. A good rep uses the full range, moves at a steady speed, has no swinging, keeps your back in the same position and causes no pain. Form means doing the exercise this way.
  5. Rest for 60–120 seconds between sets. Add reps first, then add weight.

Deeper reading (optional)

You do not need this for the first 12 weeks.

How muscle grows

Muscle growth, called hypertrophy, means muscle cells get bigger. It happens when training asks more of a muscle than usual. Protein, sleep and recovery then let the body build more tissue.

Mechanical tension is the main driver. This means a muscle works hard against weight or another load near its limit. Tiny muscle tears, soreness and "the burn" are not required. More soreness does not make a session better.

Rep ranges

A rep, short for repetition, is one full movement. A set is a group of reps followed by rest. Sets of roughly 5 to 30 reps can build muscle when they are hard. In this block, stop each set when you could still do 1–3 more good reps. You train alone with no rack, so never go until you cannot finish a rep. Heavier sets build more maximum strength. This block uses 8–12 reps.

Reps in Reserve

Reps in Reserve (RIR) tells you how many more good reps you could have done. RIR 2 means you could have done two more. Most working sets, the planned hard sets after warming up, should end at 1–3 RIR. Going to your limit adds tiredness without much extra growth. Stopping with 5 or more reps left is too easy to count as hard work.

Principles for building muscle

Progressive overload. This means making training harder over time. Add weight, reps or sets. You can also slow each movement or shorten the rest. Repeating the same workout every week only maintains your current level.

Double progression. This means adding reps first and weight second.

  1. Pick a rep range, for example 8–12.
  2. Start at a weight where you reach 8 reps at 1–3 RIR.
  3. Add reps each session.
  4. When every set reaches 12 with good form, add the smallest weight jump available and go back to 8.

Protein. Protein is a nutrient that builds and repairs tissue. Eat 1.6–2.2 g per kg of body weight a day, or 0.7–1 g per lb. A 60 kg person needs 96–132 g. An 80 kg person needs 128–176 g. Spread it over 3–4 meals. The daily total matters most. See Nutrition and Supplements.

Recovery and sleep. Sleep 7 or more hours. See Recovery, Stress and Mobility.

Frequency. In this block every session works your whole body, so your legs, chest, back and middle get work in every session.

OptionExample
Full body, 3 daysMon, Wed, Fri full-body strength
Upper and lower splitMon upper, Tue lower, Thu upper, Fri lower

Training 5–6 days a week is fine if each muscle gets about 48 hours between hard sessions.

Common mistakes

  • Too much cardio while dieting can eat into muscle.
  • No progression.
  • Too little protein.
  • Too little rest.
  • Inconsistent training.

Muscles trained in this block

Back, from your shoulders to your hipsDumbbell Row, Barbell Row, DeadliftPulling strength and support

Biceps, at the front of your upper armsBarbell Curl, Dumbbell Row, Barbell RowPulling strength
Triceps, at the back of your upper armsBench Press, Dumbbell Shoulder Press, Bench DipsPressing strength
Quads, at the front of your thighsBarbell Squat, Goblet Squat, LungesLeg strength
Hamstrings, at the back of your thighsDeadlift, Barbell Squat, Goblet SquatLeg strength and balance
Glutes, in your buttocksBarbell Squat, Goblet Squat, Deadlift, LungesHip and leg strength
Core, around your stomach, sides and lower backPlank, Leg Raises, Russian TwistsStability

Other training methods

TypePurposeBeginner frequency
StrengthMuscle, bone density, joint strength, fat loss support2–4 times a week
CardioHeart and lung health, calories, recovery days2–3 times a week
HIITTime-efficient conditioning1–2 times a week, optional
MobilityRange of motion, posture, recoveryDaily or 3–4 times a week
FunctionalReal-life strength and balance1–2 times a week

Strength training: This makes muscles work against resistance from bodyweight, dumbbells, barbells, bands or machines. It suits almost everyone.

Cardio: This trains the heart and lungs. Low-Intensity Steady State (LISS) cardio includes walking, cycling and jogging at an easy, steady pace. Moderate cardio includes brisk walking, light running and dance. Endurance cardio includes long runs, rides and swims. Use cardio alongside strength training.

High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT): Bursts of 20–60 seconds of hard effort followed by rest, in sessions of 10–30 minutes. It saves time. It does not burn meaningfully more fat than other cardio.

Mobility: Stretching, yoga, foam rolling. Matters most if you sit for long hours.

Functional training: Lunges, kettlebell swings, medicine ball throws and compound lifts such as deadlifts.

Mind-body training: Yoga, Pilates and Tai Chi improve body awareness, breathing, core stability and stress control.

Exercise basics

A rep is one full movement, including the lifting (concentric) and lowering (eccentric) phases. Controlled, full-range reps build more muscle and lower injury risk.

A set is a group of consecutive reps followed by rest. "3 sets of 10" means 10 reps, rest, repeat twice.

Sets, reps and rest

  • Maximum strength: Do 3–5 sets of 3–6 reps. Use 85–95% of your one-rep maximum, the heaviest weight you can lift once. Rest 2–5 minutes.
  • Muscle growth: Do 3–4 sets of 6–12 reps. Up to 30 reps works near failure. Use a moderate weight and stop with 1–3 reps left. Rest 60–120 seconds.
  • Muscular endurance: Do 2–4 sets of 12–20 or more reps. Use a light weight and rest 30–60 seconds.

Beginners start at 8–12 reps for general strength and muscle. Too little rest cuts performance. Rest long enough to hit your target reps on the next set.

Tempo

Tempo means the speed of each part of a rep. A 3–1–1–0 tempo means 3 seconds down, a 1-second pause at the bottom, 1 second up and no pause at the top. Slower reps improve control and help you feel the muscle working. They also lower injury risk while learning. For most sessions, use 2–3 seconds down and 1 second up.

Progressive overload in practice

Raise the weight, reps or sets, shorten rest, add a session or improve form. Use double progression (above) as the default rule.

Equipment

How to Use Gym Equipment (plus full workout program and video examples) and Basic Gym Machine Rundown

EquipmentUse
DumbbellsVersatile. Isolation work like curls and compound lifts like goblet squats.
BarbellsHeavy compound lifts (squat, deadlift, bench press) with easy overload.
Machines (selectorized, cable)Fixed path for learning form, safe isolation, constant tension.
Kettlebells, bands, medicine ballsDynamic movement, warm-ups, mobility, core work.
Cardio machines (treadmill, elliptical, rower, bike)Conditioning, calories, warm-up.
BodyweightNo equipment, scalable strength.

Safety basics:

  • Warm up for 5 minutes.
  • Start light and learn the movement.
  • Form comes first. Watch tutorials or ask a trainer.
  • Put equipment down safely after each exercise.

The best equipment is the one you feel safe using regularly.

title: Nutrition and Supplements
blurb: Calories, protein and the other macros, water, meal timing and supplements.
html:
In short

  • Calories are the energy in food and drink.
  • Protein, carbohydrate and fat have different jobs in the body.
  • Your daily food totals matter more than exact meal timing.
  • Water needs rise with activity and hot weather.
  • Supplements support food, sleep and training. They do not replace them.

What to do

In this block you eat about 1,850 kilocalories (kcal) a day to lose about 0.5 kg a week. A kilocalorie is the "calorie" on food labels, a unit of energy in food and drink. How the target was set is in Fat Loss and Metabolism.

  1. Eat about 1,850 kcal a day: 120 grams (g) of protein, about 200 g of carbohydrate and about 62 g of fat. Protein is the nutrient that builds and repairs tissue.
  2. Spread the protein across 3 or 4 meals.
  3. Photograph every meal, or the receipt when you eat out, and send it to Claude. Say whether you ate alone or shared it. A shared meal counts as half. Claude estimates the calories, protein, carbs and fat, and the tracker adds up your day.
  4. Don't chase exact numbers. Photo estimates can be 20–30% off, so your weekly weight average is the real check. If it isn't falling by about 0.5 kg a week after 2 or 3 weeks, change the target with Claude.
  5. Include vegetables or fruit in 2 or more meals.
  6. Drink about 2.5–3 litres (L) of water, equal to 5 or 6 bottles of 500 millilitres (ml).

A sample day reaches about 120 g:

MealProtein
Breakfast: 3 eggsabout 18 g
Lunch: 100 g cooked chicken (palm-sized) and a cup of cooked beansabout 45 g
Snack: 2 boiled eggsabout 12 g
Dinner: 100 g cooked chicken or fish and a cup of cooked beansabout 45 g
Totalabout 120 g

A scoop of whey, about 20–25 g, can replace a snack on a busy day.

Optional creatine and protein powder

Protein powder is optional. Use it when food does not get you to 120 g. Creatine monohydrate is also optional. Take 3–5 g a day at any time, with no cycling.

Deeper reading (optional)

You do not need this for the first 12 weeks.

Calories

A calorie is a unit of energy. The body uses it for the brain, organs, movement, tissue repair, body temperature and hormones.

  • Eat less than you burn for fat loss (deficit).
  • Eat more than you burn for muscle gain (surplus).
  • Eat what you burn to maintain.

The goal sets the calorie target. How to estimate the burn is in Fat Loss and Metabolism.

Macronutrients

Macronutrients are the parts of food that provide most of its calories. The three main ones are protein, carbohydrate and fat.

Carbs are starchy and sweet foods such as rice, yam, bread, oats, plantain and fruit. Fats are found in oils, groundnuts, avocado and egg yolk.

Protein has 4 kilocalories (kcal) per gram. It builds and repairs muscle, supports hormones and immunity, and helps you feel full. Eat 1.6–2.2 g per kg of body weight each day. Sources include chicken, beef, eggs, Greek yoghurt, whey, tofu and beans.

Carbohydrate has 4 kcal per gram. It is the main fuel for workouts and the brain. Use it for the calories left after setting protein and fat. Favour fibre-rich sources such as rice, oats, potatoes, fruit, vegetables, whole grains and legumes over refined ones.

Fat has 9 kcal per gram. It supports hormones, the brain, cell structure and the absorption of vitamins A, D, E and K. It should provide 20–35% of daily calories. Sources include olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocado, eggs and fatty fish.

Fibre has 0–2 kcal per gram. It supports digestion, blood sugar and gut health. Eat 25–35 g a day from vegetables, fruit, oats, beans and whole grains.

One kilocalorie (kcal) is the "calorie" on food labels.

Example splits

  • Fat loss: high protein, moderate carbohydrate, and moderate to low fat.
  • Muscle gain: high protein, high carbohydrate, and moderate fat.
  • Maintenance: moderate protein, carbohydrate and fat.

A 2,000 kcal fat-loss day could be 150 g protein (600 kcal), 175 g carbs (700 kcal) and 77 g fat (700 kcal).

Tracking food

In this block you track by sending Claude a photo of each meal. Apps such as MyFitnessPal, Cronometer and MacroFactor do the same job if you would rather weigh and enter food yourself. Either way the method is the same: estimate your Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE), the calories you burn in a day, set targets for each macronutrient and log food against them. Tracking builds food awareness even if you stop later.

Micronutrients

Micronutrients are vitamins and minerals. They carry no calories. A deficiency, meaning too little of one, can still harm energy, immunity, bones, muscle function and mood.

NutrientFunctionSources
Vitamin AVision, skin, immunityCarrots, sweet potatoes, spinach
B vitaminsEnergy, metabolism, nervesWhole grains, eggs, meat, legumes
Vitamin CImmunity, collagen, antioxidantCitrus, bell peppers, broccoli
Vitamin DBones, hormone supportSunlight, fatty fish, fortified foods
Vitamin EAntioxidant, skin repairNuts, seeds, spinach
Vitamin KBlood clotting, bonesLeafy greens, broccoli, cabbage
CalciumBones, nerve signalsDairy, almonds, leafy greens
IronOxygen transport, energyRed meat, beans, spinach
MagnesiumMuscle relaxation, sleep, nervesNuts, seeds, dark chocolate
ZincImmunity, wound healingMeat, shellfish, legumes
Sodium and potassiumHydration, muscle contractionSalt, bananas, potatoes, leafy greens

Vitamin D deficiency is common. Supplement if you get little sun. Low magnesium or iron can cause fatigue and poor recovery.

Hydration

Mild dehydration can hurt performance, especially in heat. It can also feel like hunger or tiredness. Water regulates temperature, lubricates joints and moves nutrients.

Activity levelDaily water
Sedentary2.5–3 L, or 5–6 bottles of 500 ml
Active3–4 L or more
Intense training or hot climate4–5 L or more

Check urine colour. Pale yellow is good. Dark yellow means drink more.

Electrolytes are minerals that help muscles contract and nerves send signals. They include sodium, potassium and magnesium. Coconut water, bananas, spinach and sea salt cover most needs. Electrolyte tablets suit people who sweat heavily and endurance athletes.

Meal timing

Total daily intake matters most. For fat loss, the deficit is the priority. Timing is a small performance extra.

Meal frequency: No number of meals is best. Three meals plus a snack suits most beginners. Four to six smaller meals can steady hunger. Two or three larger meals suit fasting routines. Include protein at each meal.

Around training: Total daily protein matters most. A meal within a few hours before or after training is enough. There is no narrow period, sometimes called an "anabolic window", that you must catch.

WhenWhat
2–3 hours beforeBalanced meal of carbs, protein and some fat
30–60 minutes beforeLight snack of carbs and protein
Within a few hours afterProtein (20–40 g) and carbs (30–60 g), plus water

Examples include oats with a protein shake, or rice with chicken and vegetables. Other options are banana with peanut butter and whey, or Greek yoghurt with honey and berries. Avoid heavy fat or a lot of fibre right before training.

Fat loss: Control calories, avoid late-night binges and do not skip meals if skipping makes you overeat later.

Muscle gain: Hit daily protein and eat every 3–5 hours.

More supplement detail

Worth taking

SupplementDoseNotes
Protein powderAs needed to reach the daily targetWhey isolate digests fast. Casein digests slowly. Pea or rice protein suits vegan diets.
Creatine monohydrate3–5 g a day, any time, no cyclingOver 1,000 studies. Improves strength, power, muscle size and recovery. Safe long term.
Vitamin D31,000–2,000 international units (IU) a day, or test blood levelsHelpful with little sun exposure.
Omega-3 (fish oil)1,000–2,000 mg of combined eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) a dayUseful if you eat fatty fish less than 2–3 times a week. EPA and DHA are the two active omega-3 fats.
ElectrolytesAfter hard sessions or in heatChoose low-sugar options, or add a pinch of sea salt and lemon to water.

Be skeptical

SupplementIssue
Fat burnersMostly stimulants with small effect and side effects
Branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs)Redundant if you eat enough protein
Testosterone boostersMostly ineffective unless you are medically deficient
Detox teas and juice cleansesThe liver and kidneys already do this
Pre-workout blendsCan cause jitters, dependence or stomach upset. Use with caution.

Look for third-party testing (NSF Certified, Informed Sport) to avoid banned or contaminated products.

Starter kit by goal

GoalKit
Fat lossWhey, electrolytes, omega-3, vitamin D
Muscle gainWhey, creatine, omega-3, vitamin D
EnduranceElectrolytes, creatine, carbohydrate drink for long sessions

The optional detail above covers the 2,000 kcal macronutrient example, vitamins and minerals, detailed water needs, meal timing and supplements beyond creatine and protein powder. You do not need that detail to follow this block.

title: Recovery, Stress and Mobility
blurb: Sleep, rest days, stress, and mobility and stretching.
html:
In short

  • Recovery is the rest that lets your body repair after training.
  • Sleep for 7 or more hours.
  • This block has one full rest day on Sunday and three walk days.
  • Work, poor sleep, hard training and eating too little all add stress.
  • Mobility work helps you move your joints with control.

What to do

  1. Sleep for 7 or more hours. Keep a regular sleep and wake time, use a dark room at 18–20°C, stop screens an hour before bed, avoid caffeine after 2 pm and eat a light dinner.
  2. Keep Sunday as the one full rest day. Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday are brisk walk days. Brisk means you can talk but not sing.
  3. Use box breathing when stressed. Breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 4, breathe out for 4, hold for 4, and repeat for 2 minutes.
  4. Do the warm-up and cool-down in Current Program. Mobility means moving a joint through its full range under your own control, like circling your hips. Flexibility means how far a joint can be stretched when something else pulls it, like a hamstring stretch.

Recovery

Recovery is the rest and repair that happen after training. During recovery, muscles rebuild, the nervous system resets and hormones settle. Muscle growth and fat loss show up during this time.

Beginners rarely overtrain from lifting. When recovery fails, the usual causes are poor sleep, low food intake and life stress. Fix those before cutting training.

Sleep

Sleep is the main recovery tool. Sleep for 7 or more hours. During sleep, the body repairs muscle and stores the movement skills you practised. Most adults need 7–9 hours. The hormone detail is in Deeper reading.

Poor sleep has clear costs:

  • More hunger and cravings, because ghrelin rises and leptin falls.
  • Lower insulin sensitivity.
  • Less energy and willpower, so workouts and food choices suffer.
  • Lower training quality.
HabitBenefit
Regular sleep and wake timesSteadies the body clock
Dark, cool bedroom (18–20°C)Deeper sleep
No screens 60–90 minutes before bedLess light disruption
Pre-sleep routine (reading, stretching, meditation)Calms the nervous system
No caffeine after 2 pmFaster sleep onset
Light dinner, no heavy late mealsEasier digestion and better sleep

Signs you are not recovering

  • Constant fatigue or low motivation
  • Trouble falling or staying asleep
  • Soreness lasting more than 3 days
  • Strength or endurance stuck
  • Mood swings or short patience
  • More cravings and poor appetite control

Rest days

TypeExamplePurpose
Total restNo intense activityFull muscle and nervous system recovery
Active recoveryWalking, yoga, stretchingBlood flow and easier soreness

This block has one full rest day on Sunday and three walk days.

Stress

Stress is physical as well as emotional. Work deadlines, poor sleep, hard workouts, conflict, undereating and overtraining all add load. In healthy people, everyday stress affects body fat mostly through sleep, appetite and food choices. Clinically high cortisol is a medical matter.

Training is itself a stress. It helps when dosed well. Hard sessions with no rest, little sleep and a steep calorie deficit pile up.

Signs of too much load, even without feeling "stressed":

  • Fatigue despite sleep
  • Bloating or poor digestion
  • Irritability or brain fog
  • Poor gym performance
  • Sugar and salt cravings
  • Trouble sleeping

What helps

Breathing exercises and meditation: Try box breathing or the 4-7-8 method. Guided apps include Headspace, Calm and Insight Timer.

Nature and walks: 10–20 minutes a day in sunlight lifts mood and improves sleep.

Journaling: Write thoughts, triggers or gratitude.

Active rest: Stretching, yoga or walking.

Boundaries and downtime: Screen breaks and leisure time with no productivity target.

HabitBenefit
Sleep 7 or more hoursSteadier mood and appetite
Eat enoughAvoids hunger-driven stress
Stay hydratedBetter energy and focus
Limit caffeineLess anxiety
Laugh and socialiseLower stress
Train smartAvoid constant high-intensity sessions

Mobility and stretching

Mobility means controlling how far a joint moves. Flexibility means how far a joint can move during a stretch. Both can improve lifting form and posture. They can also ease tightness, protect joints and help you feel better. They matter most if you sit for long hours.

  • Mobility drills: Warm up for 5 minutes with the hip circles, leg swings, arm circles, shoulder rolls, cat-cow, bodyweight squats and push-ups in Current Program.
  • Static stretching: This means holding a stretch without moving. Hold each cool-down stretch for 20–40 seconds.

Deeper reading (optional)

You do not need this for the first 12 weeks. Most adults need 7–9 hours of sleep. Leptin and ghrelin affect fullness and hunger. Cortisol is involved in the stress response. Insulin sensitivity describes how well the body responds to insulin.

The 4-7-8 method is another breathing method. Breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 7 and breathe out for 8.

Foam rolling means moving a firm foam cylinder over a muscle. Do not roll the lower back, joints or bones.

ToolPlain use
Foam rollerEases muscles and supports circulation
Massage or lacrosse ballPresses small tight spots in the buttocks and upper back
Resistance bandsDeeper stretches
Percussion gunGives repeated taps to one area. Use with caution.

Warm-up and cool-down videos are in Daily Checklist and Current Program.

The optional detail above covers the 4-7-8 breathing method, foam rolling, massage balls, resistance bands and percussion guns. Box breathing is the method used in this block.

title: Tracking and Habits
blurb: What to track and why, body measures like BMI, and how habits stick.
html:
In short

  • Track a few numbers to see progress that the scale may hide.
  • Log daily habits, each workout, weekly average weight and four-week measurements.
  • Compare trends over time, not one day's result.
  • Small routines make training easier to repeat.
  • One missed day is normal. Do a missed strength session the next day and push the rest of the week back one day.

What to do

  1. Log daily steps, sleep hours, energy and whether you trained in the tracker's Log tab, or tell Claude. Send Claude a photo of every meal, or the receipt when you eat out, and say if you shared it. The tracker adds up your calories, protein, carbs and fat from the meals. A score of 1 means drained and 10 means full of energy.
  2. After each exercise, log the weight, reps in each set and Reps in Reserve. A rep is one complete movement. A set is a group of reps before a rest. Reps in Reserve means the good reps you could still do when you stopped.
  3. Weigh yourself on 2 or 3 mornings after using the bathroom. Add the weights and divide by the number of mornings. Use that weekly average, not one day's weight.
  4. Measure every 4 weeks in the morning, before eating and after the toilet. Stand relaxed and breathe out normally. Keep the tape flat and snug on your skin without pressing in. Measure your waist at the belly button and your neck just below the Adam's apple, looking straight ahead. Measure your hips at the widest part of the buttocks with your feet together, and your chest at the nipples with your arms down. Measure your arm at the widest part of the upper arm, relaxed, and your thigh at the widest part just below the buttocks. Always use the same arm and the same leg. Do each measurement twice and log the average. Follow the measurements video.

Why track

Many beginners quit because they cannot see progress, even when it is happening. Tracking gives visible proof and shows what works. It also gives you information for adjusting the plan. A weighing scale cannot show the full picture by itself.

The system

Use the fitness tracker on your phone. Log in its Log tab, or tell Claude. Each item is logged at the pace it changes. That keeps logging under a minute.

CadenceWhat to log
DailySteps, sleep hours, every meal (a photo to Claude), energy from 1–10, and whether you trained
Each sessionExercise, weight, reps in each set, and Reps in Reserve (RIR), meaning good reps you could still do
2–3 mornings a weekBody weight, judged by the weekly average
Every 4 weeksWaist, neck, hips, chest, arm and thigh measurements, plus photos

Strength: A rep, short for repetition, is one full exercise movement. Look for more reps at the same weight, more weight at the same reps, or better form. Form means doing the movement correctly and with control.

Weight: Weigh at the same time, in the morning after the bathroom. Track the weekly average, not daily swings. Water, sleep, hormones and salt or carb intake move the number.

Measurements: Use the step-by-step method above every 4 weeks. Follow the measurements video.

Photos: Same lighting, poses (front, side, back) and time of day. Visual change often shows before the scale moves.

Energy: Rate 1–10. A score of 1 means drained and 10 means full of energy. Low scores can point to poor sleep, recovery or stress.

Screening numbers

These are rough screening numbers, not a verdict about your health.

Body Mass Index (BMI): This number compares weight with height. Calculate it by dividing weight in kilograms by height in metres squared. World Health Organization (WHO) categories are underweight below 18.5, normal at 18.5–24.9, overweight at 25–29.9, and obese at 30 or above.

UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidance uses lower thresholds for people of Black African, African-Caribbean and Asian family background. It counts 23 or above as overweight and 27.5 or above as obesity. BMI cannot separate fat from muscle. A muscular person can therefore score high while healthy.

Waist-to-hip ratio (WHR): Divide your waist measurement by your hip measurement. WHO uses 0.90 or above for men and 0.85 or above for women as the cut-off for raised health risk. A high ratio means more fat around the middle. It is linked with higher risk of heart disease and diabetes, even when BMI looks normal.

Waist-to-height ratio: keep your waist under half your height, a ratio below 0.5.

Body fat estimate: The tracker estimates body fat from your waist, neck and height using the US Navy tape method (the men's formula). It can be 3 to 4 percentage points off a lab scan, so read it as a trend. If your weight rises and the body fat estimate stays flat or falls, most of the gain is muscle. If both rise, most of it is fat. For men, under 18% is a fit range, 18–24% is average, and 25% or above is high.

Sample weekly dashboard

Targets for the current block (see Current Program):

MetricTargetExample result
Strength sessions3 (2 or more to pass the week)3 of 3
Steps5,000 to 8,000 a day by block phase, hit on 4 or more days5 of 7 days
CaloriesAbout 1,850 kcal a dayWeekly average 1,800–1,950
Protein120 g a day120 g or more on 5 days
Sleep7 or more hours6 of 7 nights
EnergyAverage 7 or more8
Weight (weekly average)Down about 0.5 kg a week0.3–0.7 kg lower than last week
Waist (every 4 weeks)Trend onlyDown

Habits

Motivation fades when life gets busy or results slow. Discipline, systems and identity carry long-term fitness.

The habit loop. A cue is a signal to begin. It triggers a routine, and a reward follows. Repetition helps the brain make the routine automatic. An alarm and laid-out workout clothes can be the cue. The post-workout meal or energy lift can be the reward.

Start small.

HabitMicro version
Workout10 push-ups or a 15-minute walk
Meal prepChop one vegetable or plan one meal
SleepPhone off 30 minutes before bed

Anchor to something you already do.

Existing habitNew habit
After brushing teeth5 squats or 10 deep breaths
After making coffeePrep a protein shake
After workChange into workout clothes at once

Build identity. Say "I'm someone who trains even when I'm tired" instead of "I want to work out." Act as that person and results follow.

Track streaks and celebrate wins. A wall calendar with checked-off days works. Celebrate a first unbroken week, a heavier lift or a week of home-cooked meals. Small wins reinforce the habit.

When you miss a strength day. Do it the next day and push the rest of the week back one day. Never do strength two days in a row. A bad week does not undo progress.

StrategyKey idea
Start smallConsistency over perfection
Anchor habitsAttach to existing routines
Identity"I'm someone who works out"
Celebrate winsReinforces the behaviour
Track itWhat you measure improves
Never miss twiceMomentum beats motivation

Deeper reading (optional)

Body Mass Index, waist-to-hip ratio, waist-to-height ratio and the body fat estimate are rough screening numbers, not a verdict. The detail above keeps the category and ethnic thresholds for reference.

title: Current Program
blurb: This block's plan: the week, the exercises, the videos and the rules.
html:
In short

  • Complete three strength sessions on non-consecutive days each week.
  • Walk and do mobility work on three other days. Rest on Sunday.
  • A minimum session still counts on a bad day.
  • Add reps first. Add weight after every set reaches 12 good reps.
  • Follow the step, calorie, protein and sleep targets for the full 12 weeks.

Goal

This 12-week block runs from Monday 16 November 2026 to Sunday 7 February 2027. It starts with a lead-in weekend: Strength A on Saturday 14 November and a walk with mobility on Sunday 15 November. The A, B, C order carries on from Saturday, so Monday 16 is Strength B. Its main goal is to build a weekly training habit and move more. Fat loss and muscle gain are secondary.

What you need

You need a flat bench, a pair of dumbbells that weigh 8.5 kilograms (kg) each, a barbell with plates, a mat or towel and your Oraimo watch. A plate is a round weight fitted onto the barbell.

If you have no bench, use the floor versions in How to Do Each Exercise. If you have no barbell, use the dumbbell versions described there. The weight you log for a barbell is the bar plus all the plates. Your home bar counts as 10 kg, so 7.5 kg on each side logs as 25 kg.

The week

DaySession
MondayStrength A
Tuesday20–30 minute walk and 10 minutes of mobility
WednesdayStrength B
Thursday20–30 minute walk and 10 minutes of mobility
FridayStrength C
Saturday20–30 minute walk and 10 minutes of mobility
SundayRest

Missed a strength day? Do it the next day and push the rest of the week back one day. Never do strength two days in a row.

Minimum session: On a bad day, complete the warm-up and the first two exercises. This takes about 20 minutes and still counts.

A passing week: Complete 2 or more strength sessions and hit the daily step target on 4 or more days.

Missed session: Do it the next day and push the rest of the week back one day. Never do strength two days in a row.

Sleep: Get 7 or more hours.

Calories: Eat about 1,850 kilocalories (kcal) a day to lose about 0.5 kg a week: 120 g of protein, about 200 g of carbohydrate and about 62 g of fat. Send Claude a photo of every meal. See Nutrition and Supplements.

Protein: Eat 120 grams (g) a day. Protein is the nutrient that builds and repairs tissue. This target is about 1.6 g for each kg of body weight.

Step targets

Check steps on your Oraimo watch, or use the phone's Health app.

WeeksSteps per day
1–25,000
3–46,000
5–87,000
9–128,000

How to lift

A rep, short for repetition, is one complete movement. A set is a group of reps followed by a rest. A good rep uses the full range of the exercise at a steady speed, without swinging, changing your back position or causing pain. Form means doing the exercise this way.

Do 3 working sets of 8–12 reps. A working set is a planned set after the warm-up. Stop each set when you could still do 1–3 more good reps. You train alone with no rack, so never go until you cannot finish a rep. Reps in Reserve (RIR) is the number of good reps you could still do when you stop. Rest 60–120 seconds between sets of the same exercise, and about 2 minutes before moving to the next exercise.

Count 8–12 Lunges on each leg and 8–12 Russian Twists to each side. Do 3 Plank holds of 20–40 seconds and log the seconds. Stop a hold early if your hips start to sag.

Add reps first. When all 3 sets reach 12 good reps, add the smallest available weight and return to 8 reps. Add 2.5 kg to the barbell. With dumbbells, use a heavier pair if you have one; if not, lower each rep over 3 seconds to make the same weight harder.

title: Daily Checklist
blurb: The daily, training-day and weekly checklist.
html:
In short

  • Tick the boxes in time order through the day.
  • Use the strength-day or walk-day boxes for today's session.
  • The minimum session still counts on a bad day.
  • Review the week and take measurements at the listed times.

This list is for someone who spends most of the day sitting. On a bad day, the minimum session still counts.

Every day

  • Checked the step count on the Oraimo watch. The target in Current Program starts at 5,000 and rises to 8,000.
  • Ate about 1,850 kcal with about 120 g of protein from foods such as eggs, chicken, fish, beans, Greek yoghurt, milk or whey. See Nutrition and Supplements.
  • Sent Claude a photo of every meal, or the receipt when eating out, and said whether it was shared.
  • Drank 2.5–3 litres of water, equal to 5 or 6 bottles of 500 ml.
  • If you take creatine: had 3–5 g today, at any time, including walk and rest days.
  • Slept for 7 or more hours. Wind down: no caffeine after 2 pm, screens off an hour before bed.
  • Logged steps, sleep, energy and training in the Log tab, or told Claude. An energy score of 1 means drained and 10 means full of energy.

Strength days

Monday is Strength A, Wednesday is Strength B and Friday is Strength C. Open Current Program and How to Do Each Exercise.

  • Ate a meal 2–3 hours before, or a light snack with carbs and protein 30–60 minutes before, and drank a glass of water.
  • Warmed up for 5 minutes with arm circles, shoulder rolls, hip circles and leg swings, cat-cow, and bodyweight squats and push-ups.
  • Completed 3 sets of 8–12 reps. A rep is one complete movement, and a set is a group of reps before a rest. Stopped each set when 1–3 more good reps were still possible. You train alone with no rack, so never go until you cannot finish a rep.
  • Rested 60–120 seconds between sets and about 2 minutes before the next exercise. For Plank, completed 3 holds of 20–40 seconds and stopped early if your hips started to sag.
  • Cooled down for 5 minutes with the hamstring stretch, hip flexor and glute stretch, chest doorway stretch, and shoulder and upper back stretch. Hip flexors are at the front of your hips, and glutes are in your buttocks.
  • Ate a meal with protein within a few hours after, and drank water.

Walk days

Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday are walk days.

  • Drank a glass of water before the walk, and took a bottle if it was hot.
  • Walked for 20–30 minutes at a brisk pace, meaning you can talk but not sing.
  • Did 10 minutes of mobility, which means moving a joint through its full range under your own control.

Weekly and every 4 weeks

  • Weighed yourself on 2 or 3 mornings this week. Added the weights and divided by the number of mornings to get the weekly average.
  • Reviewed the week. A passing week has 2 or more strength sessions and the step target on 4 or more days.
  • Every 4 weeks, took measurements and photos under the same conditions.
  • If you missed a strength day, did it the next day and pushed the rest of the week back one day. Never do strength two days in a row.

title: Glossary
blurb: Every term in plain words, from BMI to working set.
html:
In short

  • Use this note when a word in the playbook is unfamiliar.
  • Each definition stands alone and points to the fuller note.
  • Abbreviations are written out before the short form appears.

A–C

Active recovery: Easy movement on a rest day, such as walking or stretching. See Recovery, Stress and Mobility.

Afterburn: The small amount of extra energy the body uses after a workout. Its longer name is Excess Post-Exercise Oxygen Consumption (EPOC). See Fat Loss and Metabolism.

Barbell: A long bar that holds round weights called plates and is usually lifted with both hands. See Current Program.

Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR): The energy your body uses at rest for breathing, the brain and the organs. See Fat Loss and Metabolism.

Bench (flat bench): A firm, level padded seat used while sitting or lying during an exercise. See Current Program.

Biceps: The muscles at the front of your upper arms. See Muscle and Training.

Body fat estimate: The share of your weight that is fat, worked out from your waist, neck and height with a tape measure. It is a trend number, about 3 to 4 percentage points either way. See Tracking and Habits.

Body Mass Index (BMI): A rough screening number that compares weight with height. Below 18.5 is underweight, 18.5–24.9 is normal, 25–29.9 is overweight and 30 or above is obese, though lower thresholds may be used for some ethnic backgrounds. See Tracking and Habits.

Body recomposition: Losing fat and gaining muscle during the same period. See Goals and Foundations.

Bodyweight exercise: An exercise that uses your own body as the resistance, such as a Plank. See Current Program.

Brisk walk: A walk fast enough that you can talk but not sing. See Current Program.

Calorie: A unit of energy in food and drink. Food labels use kilocalories (kcal), commonly called calories. See Nutrition and Supplements.

Calorie deficit, maintenance and surplus: A deficit means eating less energy than you burn, maintenance means eating about the same, and a surplus means eating more. See Fat Loss and Metabolism.

Carbohydrate: A nutrient found in starchy and sweet foods such as rice, yam, bread, oats, plantain and fruit. See Nutrition and Supplements.

Cardio: Exercise that trains the heart and lungs, such as walking, cycling or jogging. See Muscle and Training.

Centimetre and inch: A centimetre (cm) and an inch (in) measure length. One inch is about 2.5 cm. See Start Here.

Claude: The AI assistant you chat with. You can tell Claude your numbers and it logs them for you. See Start Here.

Compound exercise: An exercise that uses several joints and muscles at once, such as a squat. See Muscle and Training.

Cool-down: Gentle stretches after a training session. See Current Program.

Core: The muscles around your stomach, sides and lower back that steady your body. See Muscle and Training.

Creatine monohydrate: An optional supplement that can improve strength and muscle gain. See Nutrition and Supplements.

Curl: An exercise where you bend your elbow to lift a weight towards your shoulder. See How to Do Each Exercise.

D–L

Deadlift: An exercise where you lift a bar from the floor by pushing through your feet and straightening your hips. See How to Do Each Exercise.

Double progression: Adding reps at the same weight until every set reaches 12, then adding weight and returning to 8 reps. See Muscle and Training.

Dumbbell: A short weight held in one hand. See Current Program.

Electrolytes: Minerals such as sodium, potassium and magnesium that help muscles and nerves work. See Nutrition and Supplements.

Estimated one-rep max: An estimate of the heaviest weight you could lift once, based on a normal set. See Tracking and Habits.

Failure: The point where you cannot complete another good rep. See Muscle and Training.

Fat: A nutrient found in foods such as oils, groundnuts, avocado and egg yolk. See Nutrition and Supplements.

Fibre: The part of plant food that supports digestion and fullness. See Nutrition and Supplements.

Flexibility: How far a joint can be stretched when something else pulls it, like a hamstring stretch. See Recovery, Stress and Mobility.

Fly: An exercise where you open your arms and bring them together to train your chest. See How to Do Each Exercise.

Form: The way you position and move your body during an exercise. Good form uses a steady, controlled movement without pain. See Muscle and Training.

Glutes: The muscles in your buttocks. See Muscle and Training.

Good rep: One complete movement through the full comfortable range at a steady speed, without swinging, changing your back position or causing pain. See Current Program.

Gram (g): A small unit of weight. One thousand grams equal one kilogram. See Start Here.

Greek yoghurt: A thick yoghurt that contains protein. See Nutrition and Supplements.

Grip: The way your hands hold a weight. See How to Do Each Exercise.

Guide tab: The tracker tab that holds this playbook. See Start Here.

Hamstrings: The muscles at the back of your thighs. See Muscle and Training.

High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT): Short bursts of hard exercise with rests between them. See Muscle and Training.

Hinge: An exercise movement where you push your hips back while keeping your back steady. See Current Program.

Hip flexors: The muscles at the front of your hips that help lift your legs. See Recovery, Stress and Mobility.

Hypertrophy: An increase in muscle size. See Muscle and Training.

Isolation exercise: An exercise that mainly uses one joint and one muscle group, such as a curl. See Muscle and Training.

Kilogram (kg): A unit of weight, about the weight of a 1-litre bottle of water. See Start Here.

Lats: Large muscles along the sides of your back. See Muscle and Training.

Litre (L): A unit used for liquids. One litre equals two 500 ml bottles. See Start Here.

Log tab: The tracker tab where you save the day's numbers. See Start Here.

Low-Intensity Steady State (LISS): Easy heart-and-lung exercise at a steady pace, such as walking. See Muscle and Training.

M–R

Macronutrients: Protein, carbohydrate and fat, the food nutrients that carry energy. See Nutrition and Supplements.

Maintenance: Eating about the same number of calories as your body burns. See Fat Loss and Metabolism.

Mechanical tension: A muscle working hard against a weight or other resistance. See Muscle and Training.

Metabolism: All the processes that keep the body working and use energy. See Fat Loss and Metabolism.

Micronutrients: Vitamins and minerals needed in small amounts. See Nutrition and Supplements.

Minimum session: The warm-up and first two exercises on a difficult day. See Current Program.

Mobility: Moving a joint through its full range under your own control, like circling your hips. See Recovery, Stress and Mobility.

Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis (NEAT): Energy used for movement outside planned workouts, such as walking and chores. See Fat Loss and Metabolism.

Oraimo watch: The watch that shows your steps and sleep in its phone app. See Start Here.

Plateau: A period when progress stops after earlier improvement. See Fat Loss and Metabolism.

Plates: Round weights placed on the ends of a barbell. See Current Program.

Pound (lb): A unit of weight equal to about 0.45 kg. See Start Here.

Press: An exercise where you push a weight away from your body. See How to Do Each Exercise.

Progress tab: The tracker tab that shows your charts. See Start Here.

Progressive overload: Making training harder over time by adding weight, reps or sets. See Muscle and Training.

Protein: A nutrient that builds and repairs tissue. See Nutrition and Supplements.

Protein target: The amount of protein planned for a day. This block uses 120 g across 3 or 4 meals. See Nutrition and Supplements.

Quads: The muscles at the front of your thighs. See Muscle and Training.

Range of motion: The distance a joint and weight travel during a rep. See Muscle and Training.

Recovery: The rest and repair that happen after training. See Recovery, Stress and Mobility.

Rep: One complete exercise movement. See Muscle and Training.

Rep range: The lowest and highest planned number of reps in a set. See Muscle and Training.

Reps in Reserve (RIR): The number of good reps you could still do when you stop a set. See Muscle and Training.

Rest between sets: The pause after one set and before the next set of the same exercise. See Current Program.

Rest day: A day without hard training. See Recovery, Stress and Mobility.

Row: An exercise where you pull a weight towards your body. See How to Do Each Exercise.

S–Z

Set: A group of reps done before a rest. See Muscle and Training.

Single-leg exercise: An exercise that trains one leg at a time, such as a Lunge. See Current Program.

SMART goal: A goal that is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. See Goals and Foundations.

Spot reduction: The false idea that training one body area burns fat from that same area. See Goals and Foundations.

Squat: An exercise where you bend your hips and knees to lower your body, then stand. See How to Do Each Exercise.

Starting weight: The weight used for your first session so you can test whether it allows 8–12 good reps. See Current Program.

Step target: The number of steps planned for each day and checked on the Oraimo watch. See Current Program.

Strength training: Exercise where muscles push or pull against weight. See Muscle and Training.

Telegram: The messaging app that sends your Sunday evening weekly score. See Start Here.

Tempo: The speed of each part of a rep. See Muscle and Training.

Thermic Effect of Food (TEF): Energy used to digest food. See Fat Loss and Metabolism.

Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE): All the energy your body uses in a day. See Fat Loss and Metabolism.

Tracker: The phone page that logs steps, sleep, protein, energy and training. See Tracking and Habits.

Traps: The muscles from the back of your neck across the top of your shoulders. See Muscle and Training.

Triceps: The muscles at the back of your upper arms. See Muscle and Training.

Waist-to-height ratio: Your waist measurement divided by your height. See Tracking and Habits.

Waist-to-hip ratio: Your waist measurement divided by your hip measurement. See Tracking and Habits.

Warm-up: Easy movement before training that prepares your muscles and joints. See Current Program.

Week pass: A week with at least 2 strength sessions and the step target on at least 4 days. See Current Program.

Week tab: The tracker tab that shows today's workout. See Start Here.

Whey: A milk-based protein powder that can help you reach the daily protein target. See Nutrition and Supplements.

Working set: A planned set done after warming up. See Current Program.

title: How to Do Each Exercise
blurb: Every exercise in the plan, step by step: set-up, the movement, mistakes and easier versions.
html:
In short

Watch the video first, read the steps and start light. A rep is one complete movement. A set is a group of reps before a rest. A good rep uses the full movement at a steady speed, without swinging, changing your back position or causing pain. Good reps matter more than heavy reps.

Strength A

Barbell Squat

Works: Your quads at the front of your thighs, hamstrings at the back of your thighs, glutes in your buttocks and core around your stomach, sides and lower back.

Start with: 30 kilograms (kg). Do 3 sets of 8–12 reps.

Set up: You have no rack, so you lift the bar into place yourself. Stand over the bar and lift it from the floor to your thighs, then to your shoulders. Press it overhead with a wide grip and lower it slowly onto the meaty part of your upper back, below your neck. Reverse the same steps to put it down. If this feels unsafe, do Goblet Squat that day and log it as Goblet Squat.

Do it:

  1. Stand with your feet about shoulder-width apart and toes slightly turned out.
  2. Keep your chest up, push your hips back and bend your knees.
  3. Lower as far as you can while your heels stay down and your back stays steady.
  4. Keep your knees moving in the same direction as your toes.
  5. Push through your feet to stand.

If you cannot stand up, sit down onto the floor or bench behind you and let the bar roll off your back behind you. Only squat with clear floor behind you.

Breathe: Breathe in before you lower and breathe out as you stand.

You should feel it in: The front and back of your thighs and your buttocks.

Common mistakes:

  • Your knees collapse inwards.
  • Your heels lift.
  • Your back rounds.

Easier version: Hold one dumbbell at your chest and do Goblet Squat.

Video: Barbell Squat

Bench Press

Works: Your chest, the front of your shoulders and your triceps at the back of your upper arms.

Start with: 30 kg. Do 3 sets of 8–12 reps.

Set up: Sit at the end of the bench with the bar on your thighs. Lie back while rolling the bar to your lower chest, then press it up. If you get stuck, lower the bar to your chest, roll it down your body to your hips and sit up.

Do it:

  1. Plant your feet and keep your head, upper back and buttocks on the bench.
  2. Hold the bar a little wider than shoulder-width.
  3. Lower it with control towards your lower chest.
  4. Keep your wrists above your elbows.
  5. Press the bar up until your arms are straight.

Breathe: Breathe in as you lower the bar and out as you press.

You should feel it in: Your chest and the back of your upper arms.

Common mistakes:

  • The bar bounces off your chest.
  • Your wrists bend far backwards.
  • Your elbows point straight out to the sides.

Easier version: Lie on the floor and press the dumbbells.

Video: Bench Press

Dumbbell Row

Works: Your lats along the sides of your back, upper back and biceps at the front of your upper arms.

Start with: One 8.5 kg dumbbell. Do 3 sets of 8–12 reps on each side.

Set up: Put the dumbbell on the floor beside the bench. Put one hand and the knee on the same side on the bench. Place the other foot on the floor and pick up the dumbbell with the free hand. You use one dumbbell and train one arm at a time.

Do it:

  1. Keep your back flat and let the dumbbell hang below your shoulder.
  2. Pull your elbow towards your hip.
  3. Pause with the dumbbell beside your ribs.
  4. Lower it with control until your arm is straight.

Breathe: Breathe out as you pull and in as you lower.

You should feel it in: The side of your back and the front of your upper arm.

Common mistakes:

  • Your body twists.
  • Your shoulder shrugs towards your ear.
  • You swing the weight.

Easier version: Use a lighter dumbbell or a filled water bottle.

Video: Dumbbell Row

Dumbbell Shoulder Press

Works: Your shoulders and triceps at the back of your upper arms.

Start with: Two 8.5 kg dumbbells. Do 3 sets of 8–12 reps.

Set up: Sit upright on the flat bench. Hold the dumbbells beside your shoulders with your palms facing forwards.

Do it:

  1. Plant your feet and keep your stomach firm.
  2. Press both dumbbells overhead.
  3. Finish with your arms straight without leaning back.
  4. Lower the dumbbells to your shoulders with control.

Breathe: Breathe out as you press and in as you lower.

You should feel it in: Your shoulders and the back of your upper arms.

Common mistakes:

  • Your lower back arches.
  • You press one side faster.
  • You drop the weights quickly.

Easier version: Press one dumbbell at a time or use lighter weights.

Video: Dumbbell Shoulder Press

Plank

Works: Your core, the muscles around your stomach, sides and lower back that steady your body.

Start with: Your body weight. Do 3 holds of about 20–40 seconds.

Set up: Put your forearms on the mat with elbows under shoulders. Stretch your legs behind you and support yourself on your toes.

Do it:

  1. Make a straight line from your head to your heels.
  2. Tighten your stomach and buttocks.
  3. Keep your hips still and your neck in line with your back.
  4. Hold for 20–40 seconds. Stop the hold early if your hips start to sag.

Breathe: Take slow breaths throughout the hold.

You should feel it in: Your stomach, sides and buttocks.

Common mistakes:

  • Your hips sag.
  • Your hips rise too high.
  • You hold your breath.

Easier version: Put your knees on the floor.

Video: Plank

Strength B

Deadlift

Works: Your hamstrings at the back of your thighs, glutes in your buttocks, back and grip.

Start with: 30 kg. Do 3 sets of 8–12 reps.

Set up: Put the bar on the floor over the middle of your feet. Use the largest plates you have so the bar starts about halfway up your shins. Stand close enough for your shins to nearly touch it. Use an overhand grip, with your palms facing you and your hands just outside your legs.

Do it:

  1. Push your hips back, bend your knees and keep your back flat and chest up.
  2. Pull the bar close to your legs as you stand.
  3. Finish tall without leaning backwards.
  4. Push your hips back and lower the bar close to your legs.
  5. Place it on the floor with control.

Breathe: Breathe in before lifting and out after you stand.

You should feel it in: The back of your thighs, buttocks and back muscles.

Common mistakes:

  • Your back rounds.
  • The bar moves away from your legs.
  • You pull with bent arms.

Easier version: Hold the dumbbells by your sides and use the same hip movement.

Video: Deadlift

Incline Dumbbell Press

Works: Your upper chest, front shoulders and triceps at the back of your upper arms.

Start with: Two 8.5 kg dumbbells. Do 3 sets of 8–12 reps.

Set up: Raise one end of the bench if it adjusts. Sit with the dumbbells on your thighs, then lie back and bring them beside your chest. If the bench does not adjust, use the flat bench and log that you used it flat.

Do it:

  1. Plant your feet and keep your upper back on the bench.
  2. Press the dumbbells upwards over your chest.
  3. Finish with your arms straight.
  4. Lower the dumbbells with control until they are beside your chest.

Breathe: Breathe out as you press and in as you lower.

You should feel it in: Your upper chest and front shoulders.

Common mistakes:

  • Your lower back lifts far from the bench.
  • The dumbbells drift over your face.
  • You lower too quickly.

Easier version: Use lighter dumbbells or press them on the floor.

Video: Incline Dumbbell Press

Lunges

Works: Your quads at the front of your thighs, hamstrings at the back, glutes in your buttocks and balance.

Start with: Two 8.5 kg dumbbells. Do 3 sets of 8–12 reps on each leg.

Set up: Stand tall with one dumbbell at each side and enough clear floor in front of you.

Do it:

  1. Step forwards with one foot.
  2. Bend both knees and lower your back knee towards the floor.
  3. Keep your front knee moving in the same direction as your toes.
  4. Push through the front foot to return to standing.
  5. Change legs.

Breathe: Breathe in as you lower and out as you stand.

You should feel it in: The front thigh and buttock of the front leg.

Common mistakes:

  • Your front knee collapses inwards.
  • Your step is too short to balance.
  • Your upper body falls forwards.

Easier version: Use no weight and hold the bench lightly for balance.

Video: Lunges

Barbell Curl

Works: Your biceps at the front of your upper arms.

Start with: 20 kg. Do 3 sets of 8–12 reps.

Set up: Lift the bar from the floor to your thighs with a flat back. Stand tall and hold it with palms facing forwards.

Do it:

  1. Keep your elbows beside your body.
  2. Bend your elbows and lift the bar towards your chest.
  3. Keep your upper arms still.
  4. Lower the bar with control until your arms are straight.

Breathe: Breathe out as you lift and in as you lower.

You should feel it in: The front of your upper arms.

Common mistakes:

  • You swing your body.
  • Your elbows move forwards.
  • You drop the bar quickly.

Easier version: Curl one dumbbell at a time.

Video: Barbell Curl

Leg Raises

Works: Your core at the front of your middle and your hip flexors at the front of your hips.

Start with: Your body weight. Do the lying version for 3 sets of 8–12 reps.

Set up: Lie on the mat with your legs straight and your arms beside you. Put your hands under your buttocks if your lower back needs support.

Do it:

  1. Press your lower back gently towards the floor.
  2. Keep your legs together and lift them.
  3. Stop before your lower back lifts.
  4. Lower your legs with control without letting them drop.

Breathe: Breathe out as your legs rise and in as they lower.

You should feel it in: The front of your stomach and hips.

Common mistakes:

  • Your lower back lifts from the floor.
  • You swing your legs.
  • You lower too far to keep control.

Easier version: Bend your knees and do reverse crunches. For Bench leg raises, lie on the bench, hold its end behind your head, lower your legs past the bench edge and lift. Flutter kicks are another option.

Video: Lying Leg Raises

Strength C

Goblet Squat

Works: Your quads at the front of your thighs, hamstrings at the back, glutes in your buttocks and core around your middle.

Start with: One 8.5 kg dumbbell held at your chest. Do 3 sets of 8–12 reps.

Set up: Hold one end of the dumbbell against your chest with both hands. Stand with your feet about shoulder-width apart.

Do it:

  1. Keep your chest up and push your hips back.
  2. Bend your knees and lower between your legs.
  3. Keep your heels down and knees moving towards your toes.
  4. Push through your feet to stand.

Breathe: Breathe in as you lower and out as you stand.

You should feel it in: Your thighs and buttocks.

Common mistakes:

  • Your heels lift.
  • Your knees collapse inwards.
  • Your back rounds.

Easier version: Squat without holding a weight.

Video: Goblet Squat

Barbell Row

Works: Your lats at the sides of your back, upper back and biceps at the front of your upper arms.

Start with: 20 kg, including the bar and plates. Do 3 sets of 8–12 reps.

Set up: Lift the bar from the floor with a flat back. Push your hips back, bend your knees slightly and hold the bar below you.

Do it:

  1. Keep your back flat and chest up.
  2. Pull the bar towards your lower ribs.
  3. Bring your elbows behind you without lifting your shoulders.
  4. Lower the bar with control until your arms are straight.

Breathe: Breathe out as you pull and in as you lower.

You should feel it in: Your back and the front of your upper arms.

Common mistakes:

  • Your back rounds.
  • Your body swings.
  • The bar moves far from your legs.

Easier version: Do Dumbbell Row with one hand supported on the bench.

Video: Barbell Row

Dumbbell Flyes

Works: Your chest.

Start with: Two 8.5 kg dumbbells. Do 3 sets of 8–12 reps.

Set up: Sit with the dumbbells on your thighs, lie on the bench and press them above your chest. Keep a small bend in your elbows.

Do it:

  1. Keep the same small bend in your elbows.
  2. Open your arms out to the sides with control.
  3. Stop when you feel a comfortable chest stretch.
  4. Bring the dumbbells back together above your chest.

Breathe: Breathe in as you open and out as you close.

You should feel it in: Your chest.

Common mistakes:

  • You lower beyond a comfortable range.
  • Your elbows bend and straighten during the rep.
  • You drop the weights quickly.

Easier version: Lie on the floor to limit how far your arms lower.

Video: Dumbbell Flyes

Bench Dips

Works: Your triceps at the back of your upper arms, chest and front shoulders.

Start with: Your body weight with knees bent. Do 3 sets of 8–12 reps.

Set up: Sit on the edge of the bench with your hands beside your hips and your fingers pointing forwards towards your feet. Move your hips just off the edge and place your feet flat with knees bent.

Do it:

  1. Keep your back close to the bench.
  2. Bend your elbows and lower with control until your upper arms are about level with the floor, or less.
  3. If your shoulders hurt, skip this exercise that day.
  4. Push through your hands until your arms are straight.

Breathe: Breathe in as you lower and out as you press.

You should feel it in: The back of your upper arms.

Common mistakes:

  • Your hips move far from the bench.
  • Your shoulders roll forwards.
  • You lower into shoulder pain.

Easier version: Keep your feet closer to the bench and use your legs for help.

Video: Bench Dips

Russian Twists

Works: Your core around your stomach and sides.

Start with: No weight. Do 3 sets of 8–12 reps to each side.

Set up: Sit on the mat with knees bent and feet on the floor. Lean back slightly with your chest up and hold your hands together.

Do it:

  1. Tighten your stomach and keep your back steady.
  2. Turn your chest and hands towards one side.
  3. Return through the centre.
  4. Turn to the other side.

Breathe: Breathe out as you turn and in through the centre.

You should feel it in: The front and sides of your stomach.

Common mistakes:

  • Only your arms move.
  • Your back rounds.
  • You turn too quickly.

Easier version: Sit more upright and make a smaller turn.

Video: Russian Twists

Warm-up moves

  • Arm circles: hold your arms out and draw controlled circles.
  • Shoulder rolls: roll both shoulders up, back and down.
  • Hip circles and leg swings: circle your hips, then swing one leg forwards and backwards while holding support.
  • Cat-cow stretch: on hands and knees, slowly round and gently arch your back.
  • Bodyweight squats and push-ups: squat without weight, then press your body away from the floor or bench.

Cool-down stretches

  • Hamstring stretch: reach towards one straight leg to stretch the back of the thigh.
  • Hip flexor and glute stretch: use a lunge to stretch the front of the hip, then bring a bent leg towards the chest to stretch the buttock.
  • Chest doorway stretch: place your forearm on the door frame at shoulder height and step through gently.
  • Shoulder and upper back stretch: bring one arm across your chest and gently pull it closer.
